precepts.label: John 5:30
precepts.why:
“Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go unto him that sent me.” Who sent Jesus? Christ answers it himself: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.”

He did not come on his own errand. He was sent from his Father, and he sought only the Father's will. And that will was to gather the twelve tribes of Israel: other sheep he must bring in, that there might be one fold and one shepherd. The gathering began when Christ came and began to teach, and his death was the beginning of the twelve tribes being brought back together.

So when he says he goes “unto him that sent me”, he is going back to the Father whose will he came to do. What that will was, the prophets had already written, and Isaiah 11 shows it.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:1-3
precepts.why:
The Old Testament shows who was sent and why. “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”: that Branch is Christ, as Zechariah 6 shows. “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord.”

Then: “and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears.” That is the same exact thing Christ said in John 5:30: “as I hear, I judge”, “I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.” The Branch out of Jesse does not judge by himself; he does the will of the one who sent him.

So what did God send him to do? Keep reading in the same chapter, and verse 12 tells it: to set up an ensign, assemble the outcasts of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah. When Christ spoke in the New Testament, he was reiterating what the Old Testament already said, and the text substantiates it.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:10-12
precepts.why:
“And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.” Who are the Gentiles here? The Jews in John 7 asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” The answer is Israel, and it is proven by staying in the passage.

“the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The Gentiles that seek the root of Jesse are the outcasts of Israel, the remnant of his people.

That was God's will in sending his Son: to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. The Pharisees and chief priests were studied men. They understood this prophecy of the dispersed, which is why they asked whether he would go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles.

precepts.label: Proverbs 1:27-28
precepts.why:
“Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come.” The Old Testament already spoke it: “When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me.”

They will not. The same words Christ spoke to the Pharisees and chief priests are written in Proverbs, against those who would not hear. When Christ, the apostles and the prophets spoke in the New Testament, their conversation was reiterating what the Old Testament was saying, and they could substantiate it with the text.

precepts.label: Deuteronomy 28:64
precepts.why:
Isaiah 11 says “he shall set up an ensign for the nations”. Why for the nations? Because Israel was going to be scattered: “And the Lord shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other; and there thou shalt serve other gods, which neither thou nor thy fathers have known, even wood and stone.”

We were going to be scattered in all these nations and live as Gentiles, serving other gods. So the ensign set up for the nations is set up to “assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The ones he gathers out of the nations are Israel.

That is what the Jews meant in John 7 when they asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”? They knew the curse: Israel scattered from one end of the earth to the other.

precepts.label: Tobit 3:4
precepts.why:
Tobit shows the dispersed are Israel once again: “For they obeyed not thy commandments: wherefore thou hast delivered us for a spoil, and unto captivity, and unto death, and for a proverb of reproach to all the nations among whom we are dispersed.”

Israel disobeyed the commandments, and so was delivered for a spoil, into captivity, unto death, and made a proverb of reproach among all the nations where they were dispersed. The Pharisees understood Tobit and the dispersed, just as they understood Isaiah 11. That is why they said of Christ, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?” They knew who the dispersed were.

precepts.label: Tobit 13:5
precepts.why:
“And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he hath scattered us.” Again it uses the word nations, explaining that it was Israel being scattered among them.

The scourge is for our iniquities, but mercy comes again, and the promise is the gathering out of all nations. That is the same gathering Isaiah 11 speaks of, and the same work Christ was sent to begin: bringing the dispersed out from among the Gentiles, where they had been scattered.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 36:19
precepts.why:
Ezekiel says the same: “And I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries: according to their way and according to their doings I judged them.”

They're dispersed. Israel was scattered among the heathen and dispersed through the countries, judged according to their own ways and doings. The Pharisees and chief priests understood Ezekiel 36 and the dispersed, along with Isaiah 11 and Tobit 3. So when they asked, “Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?”, they were speaking of scattered Israel living among the heathen.

precepts.label: Acts 21:21
precepts.why:
The New Testament shows the dispersed being taught: “And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.” There were Jews among the Gentiles, and Paul was going to them.

We know from the text that the Jews were going to be dispersed among the Gentiles and live like Gentiles. Coming back to the New Testament, it shows Paul going out to find the Jews scattered among these other nations, living like Gentiles, living like strangers, living like heathens, and bringing them back to God.

This was the prophecy sent from the Old Testament: the job was to raise up the twelve tribes of Israel again. What the Jews in John 7 asked, “will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”?, is exactly what was done.

precepts.label: Psalms 95:1-7
precepts.why:
Everything Christ and the apostles spoke was already spoken in what we call the Old Testament, and they used it to substantiate their points. So when Christ says of his other sheep, “they shall hear my voice”, the psalm already said it.

“O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.” The rock of our salvation is Christ. “For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods. In his hand are the deep places of the earth”; “The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land. O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the Lord our maker.”

“For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice.” We are the sheep of his hand, and the condition is the same: if you will hear his voice. That is exactly what Christ said in John 10: “them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice.”

For all of us there was a time that we heard this voice. We heard the word of God, and it brought us to repentance, to change. Something innate in us made us acknowledge the word of God by hearing his voice and changing our life. That is how the sheep of his pasture are known.

precepts.label: Micah 2:12
precepts.why:
Christ said, “there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” The fold he was speaking in was the Jews in Jerusalem, primarily Judah, Benjamin and Levi. The other sheep, not of that fold, were the rest of Israel, and he would gather the two nations, the southern and northern kingdoms, together under one shepherd, Jesus Christ.

Micah prophesied that one fold: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.”

“all of thee” means all twelve tribes. That is the same thing Christ was saying: I have sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd. The prophecy was that all twelve tribes were going to be brought back together.

The beginning of it coming to fruition was when Christ came and began to teach, and his dying was the beginning of the twelve tribes being gathered back together. That is what his death was about: he was sent by his Father to gather the flock of Jacob into one fold.

precepts.label: John 14:15
precepts.why:
The Comforter, the Holy Ghost, “shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.” Why would we need to remember the things Christ said? Because we would be made to forget. Through slavery the nations annihilated our twelve tribes, burned our records and beat us into submission, and we forgot what Christ said.

What did he say? That he would gather his elect from the four corners of the earth. That he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. And: “If ye love me, keep my commandments.”

The Holy Spirit causes us to remember these things. If you don't remember them, you don't have the Holy Spirit on you. Keeping the commandments is the love Christ asks for, and the Spirit brings back to our remembrance who we are and what he said.

That is what is happening now: brothers and sisters waking up worldwide. Isaiah 44 promised it to Jacob, whom the Lord chose: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty”, the word upon those thirsty for the truth, and “I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring: And they shall spring up as among the grass”. The Israelites are springing up worldwide like grass.

precepts.label: Acts 4:31
precepts.why:
On the day of Pentecost “suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting”, and “they were all filled with the Holy Ghost.” That Holy Ghost was the mighty wind that filled them.

Acts 4 shows the same thing again: “And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.” The place shook, the Holy Ghost filled them, and the result was boldness.

When the apostles spoke and the Holy Ghost filled them, they were bold in what they said, because they knew what they were saying was sent of God, and they could prove it from the scriptures. That is the spirit that came on them at Pentecost: not a show, but a boldness to speak the word of God, grounded in knowing it.

precepts.label: Ecclesiasticus 48:12-13
precepts.why:
The Holy Ghost came at Pentecost as a rushing mighty wind. Sirach tells of another man covered by the wind: “Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: whilst he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.”

Look what it says next: “No word could overcome him; and after his death his body prophesied.” While the spirit of God was on him, no word could overcome him.

Men, study. When you are out in the street, there should be no word that can confound you. We should not be hearing men teaching who cannot explain basic scriptures. We are going up against, for the most part, Christians, and they don't know the Bible. We should know who we are and how to explain it: Galatians 3, Ephesians 2:11-16. This is very elementary.

When the spirit of God is on you, no word should be able to overcome you. That is what filled the apostles at Pentecost, and that is what should fill the men who go out to teach today.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:9-10
precepts.why:
At Pentecost the Holy Ghost came as a wind. Ezekiel was told to prophesy to the wind: “Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord God; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.” That is the word of God coming upon them.

“So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.”

That is what was happening in Acts. They taught, and the people came in and gathered: devout men out of every nation under heaven, the scattered of Israel, hearing the word in their own tongues and standing up again.

All of you are here because the word of God was breathed on you, and it wasn't because the people teaching were shaky. So for you men out there teaching: study to shew thyself approved. The breath that raises the slain into an exceeding great army comes through a word that is taught with power.

precepts.label: Psalms 19:3
precepts.why:
At Pentecost they “began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” Other tongues means other languages. The psalm already said it: “There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.”

There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard. The devout men dwelling at Jerusalem came “out of every nation under heaven”, because according to Deuteronomy 28 we were going to be scattered into all nations. Every man heard the apostles speak in his own language, and they marvelled, “are not all these which speak Galileans?” That is because we were scattered among the heathen and learned their languages.

So God made sure the word reached every one of them in the tongue wherein they were born. In every language the scattered people of Israel had taken on, their voice was heard, and the gathering of the twelve tribes began.

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.label: Acts 22:12
precepts.why:
Cornelius is called “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house”. What does it mean to be devout? Acts 22 shows it: “And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. To be devout is to be devout according to the law, and to have a good report for it.

So when Acts 10 says Cornelius was a devout man, it is saying he was a law-abiding man. He kept the laws of God. He feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.

His own messengers tell Peter the same thing later in the chapter: “Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews”. The same good report Ananias had among the Jews, Cornelius had too.

That is why Peter came to understand that the vision was about man, not food, and that he should not call any man common or unclean. Cornelius was a just man and a devout man, a keeper of the law. “God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.”

precepts.label: Tobit 12:15
precepts.why:
The angel tells Cornelius, “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.” How do prayers come up before God? Tobit shows it. The angel Raphael says, “I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One.”

These are the angels that bring your prayers before the Most High God. Cornelius saw “an angel of God coming in to him” about the ninth hour, and that angel came because his prayers had gone up and been presented before the Holy One.

So when Acts 10 says his prayers and alms came up “for a memorial before God”, it is speaking of this very thing: the holy angels going in and out before the glory of God, presenting the prayers of those who fear him.

And the answer came back down by the same way. The angel told Cornelius to send men to Joppa and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter, who would tell him what he ought to do.

precepts.label: Tobit 12:8
precepts.why:
In the same chapter where Raphael says he presents the prayers of the saints, he says what makes those prayers go up: “Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness.” Prayer joined with fasting and alms and being righteous is what makes your prayers go before the Lord.

In other words, when you pray to God and combine it with alms and fasting, the prayers are heard before the Most High. That is exactly what we read of Cornelius in Acts 10:2: “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.”

And it is exactly what the angel told him in Acts 10:4: “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.” Not his prayers alone, but his prayers and his alms together, from a devout man who kept the law.

So Cornelius is the example of what Tobit teaches. His righteousness, his alms and his praying alway went up before God, and God answered by sending him to Peter.

thread.label: Acts 10:1
thread.text: There was a certain man in Cesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band,

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.label: Joshua 17:7
precepts.why:
Where is Cornelius from? Some people say Italy. He is from Cesarea. There are three Caesareas: one in Africa, which is not written of, Caesarea Philippi, and Caesarea Maritima. Cornelius is from Caesarea Maritima, the place the maps call Strato's Tower, right under Dor, in Samaria, the same country where Christ spoke to the woman at the well. When Rome colonized our land they named it for Caesar, and Maritima because it is a port on the water. And the maps mark that land West Manasseh.

Somebody will say that's just a map, it ain't in the Bible. So here it is in the Bible, for the doubters: “And the coast of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethah, that lieth before Shechem; and the border went along on the right hand unto the inhabitants of En–tappuah.”

Read on. “Now Manasseh had the land of Tappuah: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim”. The coast went down to the river Kanah: “the coast of Manasseh also was on the north side of the river, and the outgoings of it were at the sea”. “Southward it was Ephraim’s, and northward it was Manasseh’s, and the sea is his border”: the Mediterranean Sea. Peter dwelt in Joppa and went some thirty to forty miles up the coast to Caesarea Maritima, just before Dor.

Then verse 11: “And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Beth–shean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns”. Under Dor was Caesarea Maritima; that was all Dor before. Endor, Taanach and Megiddo were Manasseh's too. “Yet the children of Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants of those cities; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.” There were too many of them to conquer them all.

So that is Manasseh's land. It is called West Manasseh because Manasseh also dwelt on the other side of Jordan, East Manasseh. This was once Manasseh's allotment right under Ephraim, the sons of Joseph. Asher shared that port, but the land was Manasseh's.

Cornelius was not Italian. He was of the Italian band, a unit of the Roman army. There were Israelites in Rome's military, just as there are Israelites in America's military today. But negroes love master so much they see the word Italian and get excited: yes, he's white, I knew it. No, he was of the Italian band, from Caesarea, West Manasseh, one of the northern kingdom. A centurion was over a hundred men. He was “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway”, the exact same thing Tobit said he did.

thread.label: Acts 10:9-19
thread.text: On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.label: Hosea 12:10
precepts.why:
Peter fell into a trance and saw a vessel full of “fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air”, and a voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” Peter answered, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” But the vision was not really talking about food. That is why it says “Peter doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen should mean”.

When visions come from God, they are an allegory, referring to something else many times. The Lord proves it himself: “I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets.” A similitude shows you one thing, but it is really something else he is trying to explain.

That is what Peter was pondering. Is the Lord telling me to eat unlawful animals? No, Lord, I have never eaten anything unlawful. The beasts in the sheet were a similitude, and Peter did not yet know what they stood for.

He found out when he came to Cornelius. He said, “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” The vision was not about unclean animals; it was about man. Cornelius was a just man and a devout man, and the vision was showing Peter that God is no respecter of persons, northern kingdom or southern kingdom: “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” Israel, the ones called not God’s people, would one day be joined back in.

thread.label: Acts 10:11-12, the vessel decoded
thread.text: And saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth:

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common
Recovering the Remnant: Worldwide Blitz

precepts.label: Hosea 8:8
precepts.why:
Peter “saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners.” Now the scriptures substantiate the vision he had. What is the vessel? Hosea says: “Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.”

Israel was that vessel, a vessel among the Gentiles in which nobody had pleasure. Swallowed up among the nations, Israel was not wanted by anyone.

This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear Acts 10, they think it is everybody. No. God said Israel was the vessel. Peter's vision was not about the whole world coming in; it was about the scattered house of Israel, living among the Gentiles, being let down before him so that it could be gathered.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:12
precepts.why:
The vessel in Peter's vision was “knit at the four corners.” The four corners are in the prophets too: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

So what is in that sheet, gathered at the four corners? It was Israel, scattered through the four corners of the earth, living as beasts. The outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah are the ones God assembles from those four corners.

He sets up an ensign “for the nations” because Israel would be scattered among all the nations and live as Gentiles. The picture of a sheet knit at four corners is the picture of God drawing his scattered people together from every end of the earth, and that is the vision Peter had to explain to those of the circumcision.

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 8:29
precepts.why:
In the vessel were “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.” Peter had to explain to the circumcision, who contended with him, that the fourfooted beasts, the wild beasts, the creeping things and the fowls of the air refer to man. So there had to be scripture to prove it.

Ezra prays: “Let it not be thy will to destroy them which have lived like beasts; but to look upon them that have clearly taught thy law.” There are men who have lived like beasts, and Ezra pleads with God not to destroy them. So we know the beast refers to man.

The vision was not about animals; it was about men. Israel, scattered and living like beasts without the law, is what was let down in that sheet, and Ezra's prayer is that God would spare them and look upon those who teach his law.

precepts.label: Psalms 73:22
precepts.why:
Another witness that the beasts in Peter's sheet are men: the psalmist says of himself, “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.”

A man, foolish and ignorant before God, is called a beast. So when Peter explained the vision to those of the circumcision who contended with him, he could say: remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts before God.

That is the whole key to Acts 10. The fourfooted beasts in the vessel are not pork and shellfish made clean. They are the people of Israel who were foolish and ignorant, living as beasts before the Lord, whom God was now going to cleanse and gather back together.

precepts.label: Isaiah 51:20
precepts.why:
The vessel also held “wild beasts.” Isaiah names them: “Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the Lord, the rebuke of thy God.”

The sons of Israel, fainted and lying at the head of every street, are compared to a wild bull caught in a net, full of the fury of the Lord. The wild beast is a man of Israel under God's rebuke.

When Peter explained the fourfooted beasts and wild beasts, he would have to refer to scriptures like these. Remember, it is written in 2 Esdras that we lived as beasts. Remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts. Remember, Isaiah the prophet said we would be as a wild bull. The vision was about men, and the scriptures prove it.

precepts.label: Habakkuk 1:14
precepts.why:
The vessel also held “creeping things.” Who are the creeping things? The vision was not about animals; it was about man, so there has to be a scripture showing that the creeping thing refers to man. Habakkuk says to God: “And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?”

Men made as creeping things that have no ruler over them. When we were without God, with no ruler, we were like creeping things, like insects or bugs. Without the laws of God, we were like beasts, like animals.

So every creature in Peter's sheet is a description of Israel scattered without God and without his law. The creeping things are men with no ruler over them, and God was about to bring them back under his rule.

precepts.label: Hosea 7:11-12
precepts.why:
The last creatures in the vessel are the “fowls of the air.” There had to be scripture to show that the fowls of the air also refer to man. Hosea says: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria. When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard.”

Ephraim, the northern kingdom, is the silly dove, brought down as the fowls of the heaven. So the fowls in Peter's vision are Israelites too.

Now imagine those of the circumcision hearing Peter speak: listen, over here in Hosea, remember, God called us fowls. God was showing him it was time to gather the twelve tribes, north and south, back together.

That is why the scripture says prove all things. Everything must be proven as it is written, that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and overcome when thou art judged. Peter did not just tell a vision; he could prove every creature in it from the prophets.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:22
precepts.why:
Peter says, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. That phrase “another nation” might throw you off, because Christians use it to say Peter was going to other races. Ezekiel shows what that other nation is: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”.

The kingdom of Judah was called a nation, and the kingdom of Israel, Ephraim and the rest, was called a nation. Two nations, two separate kingdoms, but one people. So when Peter the Jew, of Judah, speaks of coming unto one of another nation, that other nation is the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. That is what the vision of the sheet was about: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean”, speaking of Cornelius and his family.

Then Peter says God “is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” A Christian will stop you right there, but read the next verse: “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”. That tells you who Cornelius and his kinfolk were: the children of Israel, scattered in every nation.

Acts 15 looks back on this and quotes the prophets: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. The regathering of the twelve tribes, the two kingdoms coming back together, is what Acts 10 is about. God is bringing the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom back into one nation, just as Ezekiel said.

thread.label: Acts 10:13, rise, kill, and eat
thread.text: And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.label: Baruch 5:5
precepts.why:
We know now the vision is referring to man. So what is the “Rise” talking about? What was the whole purpose of the vision? To gather the northern and southern kingdoms back together, to gather us back from where we were scattered, east to west, north and south.

Baruch uses the same word: “Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west unto the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of God.” The children are coming from the west unto the east, and they rejoice when they remember God.

They are gathered “by the word of the Holy One.” That word is what is going to gather the children of Israel back together. This is it right here.

So when the voice says “Rise, Peter”, he is telling Peter: it is time. Awake. Rise. Now it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. The arising comes first; then comes the kill and the eat, because before we gather the twelve tribes we first have to be made ready to teach them.

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 8:12
precepts.why:
“Rise, Peter; kill”. What does kill mean? A brother answered: kill the old man, the old mindset, as it is written in Romans 6. That is right. But in that time there was no New Testament. Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

Ezra gives it: “Thou broughtest it up with thy righteousness, and nurturedst it in thy law, and reformedst it with thy judgment. And thou shalt mortify it as thy creature, and quicken it as thy work.” That is what you do. You have to mortify, deaden, kill the old man, and be quickened as God’s work.

That is the “kill” in Peter’s vision. Rise, Peter, and kill the old man. Mortify yourself. Discipline yourself. The man God brings up in his righteousness, nurtures in his law and reforms with his judgment is the man who has put the old man to death.

Only after the old man is killed can you eat, learn the scripture, and then go out and teach. That is the order God gave Peter before sending him to gather the northern kingdom.

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 8:4-5
precepts.why:
After “kill” comes “eat”. What does eat mean? Learn the scripture. Ezra says it plainly: “Swallow then down, O my soul, understanding, and devour wisdom.” That is the eating. You have to go out and learn.

And after you learn, what do you do? “For thou hast agreed to give ear, and art willing to prophesy: for thou hast no longer space than only to live.” You gave ear, you devoured wisdom, and now you are willing to prophesy. After you learn, you go out and prophesy.

So the whole vision is laid out. Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel back together. Kill, Peter: kill the old man, mortify yourself. Eat, Peter: devour wisdom. Then go out and prophesy.

This is the Old Testament way Peter would have explained it to those of the circumcision: the eating in the vision was never about unclean beasts, but about swallowing down understanding so he could teach the scattered of Israel.

precepts.label: Revelation 10:9-11
precepts.why:
Revelation says the same thing. John went to the angel and said, “Give me the little book. And he said unto me, Take it, and eat it up; and it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey.” John “took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it up”, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth, and as soon as he had eaten it his belly was bitter.

Then comes the reason for the eating: “Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings.” The book is eaten so that it can be prophesied.

That is the same pattern as “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” You have to eat, you have to learn, and then you must go out and prophesy. John ate the book and was sent before many peoples and nations; Peter was told to eat and was sent to the house of Cornelius.

So eating in the vision means taking in the word. Rise, kill the old man, eat the word, and go out and prophesy to the scattered tribes.

thread.label: Acts 10:14-15, common and unclean
thread.text: But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.label: Ecclesiastes 6:1
precepts.why:
Peter answered the vision, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” To understand what he meant by common, go to Solomon: “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men”.

Common is tied to evil. Peter understood that. So when he said he had never eaten anything common, he was not only talking about meat. In other words: I have never done sin, I have never dealt with sin, I have never dealt with people that were evil.

That is why the vision had to be explained to him. The sheet let down from heaven was not about food; it was about men, and Peter was being told to go among people he had counted as common.

precepts.label: Baruch 6:11
precepts.why:
Baruch shows the word common used again for evil. Speaking of the idolaters and their gods, “they will give thereof to the common harlots, and deck them as men with garments, being gods of silver, and gods of gold, and wood.” The common harlots: the word goes with whoredom and idolatry.

So when Peter said, “I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean”, he was saying, I have never dealt with sinners. I have never sat down with them.

But then the voice spake unto him again the second time, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” What had God cleansed? The subject matter is man. And to explain that cleansing to those of the circumcision, Peter would have to go to the Old Testament: to Ezekiel 37, where God would save them out of their dwelling places and cleanse them, take the children of Israel from among the heathen and make two kingdoms one; and to Hosea 1, where in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, it would be said, Ye are the sons of the living God.

The time had come to gather the northern kingdom back together. And that is happening now: God's people are being gathered in South America, in Africa and here in the States.

thread.label: Acts 10:15
thread.text: And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.label: Hosea 8:8
precepts.why:
Peter saw “a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners”. A vessel knit at the four corners. Remember the Lord told Jacob his children would be scattered abroad to the north, east, south and west. Hosea says what that vessel is: “Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.”

A vessel wherein is no pleasure means unclean, no good, unable to be used. Vessels were used in the temple for service, but a vessel in which there is no pleasure cannot be used for temple service; it is deemed unclean. That is Israel scattered among the nations, counted unclean.

So the vessel full of “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air” is Israel scattered to the four corners and swallowed up among the Gentiles. Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” But “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” It is not talking about no damn animals; it isn't about pork.

At Hezekiah's Passover many of Ephraim and Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun “had not cleansed themselves”, yet Hezekiah prayed, “The good Lord pardon every one That prepareth his heart to seek God”, and “the Lord hearkened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.” Cornelius, of West Manasseh, was a devout man who prepared his heart to seek God. God cleansed that vessel of no pleasure, and Peter learned he “should not call any man common or unclean.”

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:12
precepts.why:
The sheet Peter saw was “knit at the four corners”, and Isaiah shows why: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

The nations here are Israel. He will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah, as Hosea said, from the four corners of the earth. A vessel knit at the four corners: that is Israel scattered to every corner, and the Lord gathering them.

That is what the vision meant. Peter doubted in himself what it should mean, thinking what Christians think, that he was told to eat unclean food. But he saw it three times, and three men came from Cornelius. Then he understood: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” The vision was about a man, Cornelius, one of the outcasts of Israel from the northern kingdom whom Judah called common and unclean.

What God hath cleansed, call not thou common: the Lord is gathering both houses, the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah, and making them clean, one nation again, as Ezekiel said, “neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”.

thread.label: Acts 10:21-28
thread.text: Then Peter went down to the men which were sent unto him from Cornelius; and said, Behold, I am he whom ye seek: what is the cause wherefore ye are come?

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

thread.label: Acts 10:28
thread.text: And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:22
precepts.why:
Peter said, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. Sound familiar? It is the same thing the woman at the well said to Christ: the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. “but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean”. Any man, not food, not animals. The vision was about a man, Cornelius.

Who is one of another nation? In Genesis 35 Jacob was told a nation and a company of nations would come of him. Ezekiel shows the two becoming one: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”. Judah and Ephraim, both the houses, gathered together under one king.

“Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions: but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.” He will cleanse both kingdoms and make them clean.

So Cornelius was of another nation, another kingdom: the northern kingdom. Judah called the northern kingdom common and unclean, not my people, strangers. But what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. God promised to cleanse them and make the two one nation, and that is why Peter could go into Cornelius's house.

thread.label: Acts 10:34-35
thread.text: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:

classes.title: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.label: Acts 2:1-5
precepts.why:
Peter says, “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” Every nation: Acts 2 shows who was in every nation. “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.”

They had come together for the feast of Pentecost: “And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.” These were devout Jews, devout like Cornelius, gathered out of every nation where they had been scattered. So “every nation” in Peter’s words is not every race of people; it is the Israelites living in every nation under heaven.

And God received them. “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind”, “cloven tongues like as of fire” sat upon each of them, “And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.”

That is what Peter came to understand at Cornelius’ house. God is no respecter of persons, northern kingdom or southern kingdom. Those that keep the commandments have a place of repentance, and Israel, the ones that were called not God’s people, would one day be joined back in.

thread.label: Acts 10:35
thread.text: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.label: Acts 2:5
precepts.why:
Peter said, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” In every nation, because Israel is in every nation. Luke shows it at Pentecost: “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.”

Israel is scattered everywhere, to all four corners: that is the vessel knit at the four corners in Peter's vision. So “in every nation he that feareth him” is not every people on earth; it is the Israelites scattered in every nation who fear God and work righteousness, like Cornelius, a devout man who feared God with all his house and gave much alms.

And read the next verse; they always skip it. “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”. The word was sent to the children of Israel. Those accepted in every nation are the children of Israel in every nation.

precepts.label: Joel 2:32
precepts.why:
Peter told Cornelius, “To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.” Isn't that what Cornelius was receiving? Joel is one of the prophets giving that witness: “And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered”.

That word whosoever again. But where is the deliverance? Not in all the heathen nations: “for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the Lord hath said, and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”

The whosoever is the remnant whom the Lord shall call. Peter said to Cornelius, “That word, I say, ye know”: the Samaritans and the northern kingdom knew it, as Isaiah said Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria shall know, and as the woman at the well said, I know that Messias cometh. Cornelius was devout; he knew the law and that he would be called eventually. He was of that remnant.

precepts.label: Luke 1:68
precepts.why:
“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”. The Lord God of Israel visited and redeemed his people, not every people.

Read on to verse 77: “To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins”. To whom? Unto his people. Remission of whose sins? Their sins.

So the word Peter brought to Cornelius was for the remission of their sins, and that includes Cornelius too. “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him” because Cornelius was one of his people, an Israelite of the northern kingdom in West Manasseh, whom the Lord God of Israel came to visit and redeem. Acts 15 says it: “God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.” That visit, beginning with Cornelius, is the building again of the tabernacle of David, all twelve tribes reunited.

precepts.label: Deuteronomy 4:27
precepts.why:
“Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.” When the Bishop says separate that brother for the work, he is not talking about Atlanta. He is not talking about Miami or California. Did Israel only scatter in Atlanta? Did Israel only scatter in America? Separate them for the work means no matter where the work is, you have to go there.

The prophecy shows where the work is: “And the Lord shall scatter you among the nations”. Not in America, not in Florida: among the nations. “and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen, whither the Lord shall lead you.” You know what that scripture is saying? No matter where you go, you are going to see Israelites. That is why a judge must be able to travel. Captain Joham just came from Trinidad and Suriname keeping Passover with the brothers there.

So the work Barnabas and Saul were separated for is the same work now: going to the nations where the Lord scattered Israel. It was the Most High God who called you, not the bishop, deacon or captain, and once hands are laid on you, you are sent away. When the phone call comes to travel, we do not want to hear anything from you but yes. Paul travelled, departing unto Seleucia and sailing to Cyprus, and we continue the Acts of the Apostles, bringing the good news all over the world, whatever hate we get for it.

thread.text: Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to th

precepts.label: Matthew 4:15
precepts.why:
Paul and Barnabas tell Judah, “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”, but the scribes and them were rejecting it, so “lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” Before that, those scattered abroad after the persecution about Stephen were “preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only”: only to the tribe of Judah. So who are the Gentiles they turned to?

Matthew answers it: “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles.” Zabulon and Nephthalim are tribes of the northern kingdom, and the scripture calls them Gentiles. When Paul and Barnabas turned to the Gentiles, they turned to the northern kingdom Israelites.

That is what the vision of Peter in Acts 10 was about. Peter said “it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. Christians use that to say other races, but Ezekiel shows the two kingdoms were two nations: “they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.” Judah was a nation and the kingdom of Israel, Ephraim and the rest, was a nation. And Peter’s own words about Cornelius and his kin folk are “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”.

Acts 15 looks back on Acts 10: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. The kingdom was split, Judah, Benjamin and Levi on one side, Ephraim and the rest on the other. Turning to the Gentiles is God bringing the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom back together, the regathering of the twelve tribes.

thread.text: Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.

classes.title: Pope Nicholas & the Moors of Spain

precepts.label: Amos 9:11
precepts.why:
Isaiah spoke of “the day that the Lord bindeth up the breach of his people, and healeth the stroke of their wound.” What does it mean to bind up the breach of his people? Acts 15 answers it. “Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name. And to this agree the words of the prophets”: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. That is bringing back the twelve tribes of Israel.

James was quoting Amos: “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof”. Closing up the breaches is the binding up of the breach in Isaiah 30: when he gathers the twelve tribes of Israel back again. Right now the tabernacle is still fallen; we are trying to gather ourselves together. “and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old”.

“That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name”. Possess means own. We are going to own the remnant of Edom and all the nations. The heathen called by his name are those who call themselves Jews and Christians. Jew comes from Judah, which means praise of God, so Amalek is saying they are the praise of God, and they're not. Christian means anointed ones, calling themselves God's anointed. All of them that call themselves by those names, we are going to possess, “saith the Lord that doeth this”: he is going to make sure that thing is done.

precepts.label: Isaiah 60:12
precepts.why:
Simeon's words, “That the residue of men might seek after the Lord”, can be confusing. How are they going to seek after the Lord? Isaiah answers it: “For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted.”

They will seek after the Lord in captivity. There is no we're equal to you, we're ruling with you. The nations don't get a pass for all the evil they did. They are going to learn God's laws, his statutes and his commandments, and they will learn them in slavery, serving Israel. Whoever does not want to follow it shall be put to death. That is what the Bible says.

People online say the door is open for everyone, that God is going to take everybody in the same way. They don't understand. The residue of men seek the Lord by serving the kingdom of Israel, and the nation or kingdom that will not serve shall perish and be utterly wasted.

precepts.label: Zechariah 14:16
precepts.why:
Here is more on how the residue of men will seek after the Lord: “And it shall come to pass, that every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles.”

What do they have to keep? The feast of tabernacles. The nations that are left will worship the King and keep the feast. When is the feast of tabernacles? The seventh month, the fifteenth day. So we are going to have to teach that to the nations: in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day, you go up towards Jerusalem to worship the King and you keep the feast of tabernacles.

That is what it means that the residue of men seek after the Lord. They come up under Israel, learning and keeping God's law, the law they would not keep before. It does not contradict Amos 9:12; it says the same thing. Amos just made it plain, while the way Simeon put it leaves people asking what it means.

precepts.label: Zechariah 14:17
precepts.why:
There may be some rebellious heathen out there: “And it shall be, that whoso will not come up of all the families of the earth unto Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, even upon them shall be no rain.”

That is judgment. No rain means famine, no rain means dearth, no rain means death. Read on: “And if the family of Egypt go not up, and come not, that have no rain; there shall be the plague, wherewith the Lord will smite the heathen that come not up to keep the feast of tabernacles.”

So when Acts 15 says “That the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called”, it is not an open door where everyone is equal. The residue of men will seek the Lord in servitude, keeping the feast, and those who refuse get no rain and the plague. And the Gentiles upon whom his name is called, those who call themselves Jews and Christians, God's praise and God's anointed: chains for them.

precepts.label: Lamentations 2:13
precepts.why:
Paul proves from the Psalms that Israel became filthy: “They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one.” The whole nation was broken. Jeremiah laments that same breaking: “What thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee?”

A breach is a split or a tear. Our breach is great like the sea. Who can heal us? Christ, our saviour.

Isaiah shows the healing: “And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.” When our souls are in drought, the Lord is going to water us and heal us. “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places”, the waste places we made when we became filthy. “Thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.”

The root word of reparations is repair. The repairer of the breach: that is the reparations right there. Both Jews and Gentiles, Judah and Ephraim, were “all under sin” and torn apart, and the one who heals that breach is Christ, repairing and restoring Israel.

precepts.label: Acts 15:14-17
precepts.why:
Paul says “we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”, and the Gentiles there are Israelites. Acts 15 shows the same Gentiles being restored: “Simeon hath declared how God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.” That references what took place in Acts 10, and we understand that is talking about Israel.

“And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written, After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up”. Build again: that is the reconciliation, that is the reparation. It had fallen down because we became filthy, and God restores the waste places. Who is that? All twelve tribes of Israel.

Then verse 17: “That the residue of men might seek after the Lord”. The residue is the rest of the nations outside of the twelve tribes: Edom and the others. “And all the Gentiles, upon whom my name is called”: that is the Christians, and the Jews.

They try to include themselves in our reconciliation, our restoration and our adoption. But the building again is of David’s tabernacle, the twelve tribes; the residue only seeks after the Lord once Israel is set up again.

precepts.label: Amos 9:11-12
precepts.why:
Acts 15 quotes the prophet Amos: “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof”. The breaches are the tear, the split, like the breach “great like the sea” in Lamentations. Remember, the root word of reparations is to repair.

“And I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old”. This is the restoring of Israel, both kingdoms that Paul proved “are all under sin” in Romans 3, repaired and raised up as in the days of old.

Then: “That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name, saith the Lord that doeth this.” That they, all twelve tribes, may possess the remnant of Edom and of the heathen called by his name.

So you see, other nations cannot be involved in our reconciliation, our restoration or our reparation. The ones called by his name, the Christians and the Jews, are not the tabernacle being raised; they are what Israel possesses once it is raised. This goes back to the classes before on Romans 11 and Acts 10.

thread.label: Romans 4:1-8
thread.text: What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?

classes.title: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.label: Nehemiah 10:33
precepts.why:
Romans 4:2 says “For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.” What works is Paul talking about? Nehemiah condenses them into one verse: “For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.”

Continual means it was done all the time, daily, annually. And “to make an atonement” goes back to the word justify: atone, justify and reconcile are the same thing. So the works Paul is talking about are temple sacrifice, temple law. When Paul wrote, the temple was still standing and the Jews in Rome were still going to it and still sacrificing, and they believed their works were enough.

Abraham shows the order. In Genesis 15 the Lord promised the old man an heir out of his own bowels and seed as the stars, “And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” He was promised the land and he believed. Only then was he told to take the heifer, the goat, the ram and the birds and divide them. Faith came first, then the works.

When brothers don't study Paul's letters, they start saying Paul's letters are not authoritative, and speak evil of dignities, of Paul, Mark and Luke, because they weren't of the twelve. When you speak evil of dignities, your mind is blinded and you end up teaching a whole different gospel: that the nations can be saved. House negroes are the worst kind of negro. But this is the college course of this school. Know what the works are from Nehemiah, and nobody can come to your school or camp and confound you at Romans 4.

precepts.label: Hebrews 10:28
precepts.why:
Romans 4:4 says “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.” To him that offers sacrifices, the reward is not reckoned of grace or mercy, but of debt, because under Moses there was no grace. Hebrews shows it: “He that despised Moses’ law died without mercy under two or three witnesses”. Without mercy means without grace.

If you chose to do something worthy of death that an animal could not atone for, you had to die. If you broke the Sabbath, you couldn't atone with an animal. Homosexuality, you couldn't atone with an animal. Idolatry, you couldn't atone with an animal. And if you chose not to sacrifice at all, you had to die. So you were indebted to offer continual sacrifices all the time: continual burnt offerings, drink offerings, sin offerings.

The prophets said the temple would be destroyed. Once the temple is gone, where are your works? If your salvation rests on sacrificing an animal and there is no animal, no priest and no temple to atone with, by default you have condemned yourself. That is why faith in Christ has to supersede the works.

“But to him that worketh not”, him that does not offer sacrifice, “but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” Christ justifies the ungodly through his death. Just as with Abraham, who was counted faithful before he sacrificed animals, God “imputeth righteousness without works”. Israel could keep sacrificing while the temple stood, but Christ had to come first in their minds, or they were in debt.

thread.label: Romans 4:19-25
thread.text: And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara’s womb:

classes.title: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.label: Isaiah 53:4-12
precepts.why:
Paul says Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” Our offences: whose? Isaiah 53 shows who Christ was delivered for. “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows”: this is Isaiah speaking of his people. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Maybe you are thinking that is everybody. Keep reading.

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Like sheep of the house of Israel. The us is the sheep. “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth”; he did not say one word. Then: “for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” Not all people, not all nations, not the good nations, not the not-so-bad ones. My people. And Isaiah was an Israelite. Now you know who the our is, who the all is, who the we is.

All the apologists online have to do is show us in the Old Testament where this changed and Christ came back a second time and died for heathens. Show where Isaiah says, oh yeah, I almost forgot the other nations. Peter said the unlearned and unstable wrest Paul’s letters as they do the other scriptures, but this is what Paul got it from.

“By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.” Many who? Israelites; the thought has not changed. “He bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” An intercessor is a mediator, someone who steps in and dies in your place. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for the other nations. Abraham believed without the works of sacrifice, and so must we: faith in the one delivered for our offences.

precepts.label: Daniel 9:24-26
precepts.why:
Christ was delivered for our offences. Daniel shows the same thing on the prophetic clock: “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”. Seventy weeks, 490 years, upon thy people: Daniel’s people, Israel.

For what? “To finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.” That is what Christ did when he died. Reconciliation goes back to the word atonement, and back to the word justification.

“From the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem”: the rebuilding under Persia. “Unto the Messiah the Prince”: Rome. “And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”. He would be killed, but not for himself. Who was he killed for? His people. That is what Isaiah said, and that is why Daniel says not for himself.

“And the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”: Titus and Vespasian. “And the end thereof shall be with a flood”: war, 70 AD. “And unto the end of the war desolations are determined”: Israel removed out of the land and scattered among all nations into slavery. When the temple was destroyed there was no priest and no temple left to atone with, so the one who put his faith in the animal instead of Christ condemned himself by default. Faith in Christ had to come first.

precepts.label: Isaiah 45:25
precepts.why:
Isaiah 53 says “by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many”. Somebody says, see, many means anybody. Isaiah has something for that: “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.”

Not all the seed of Israel and anybody else outside of Israel. Not all the good nations. Not individual heathens who say they have black friends. All the seed of Israel, all twelve tribes, shall be justified.

How? My righteous servant justifies many by dying on the cross, by laying on himself the iniquity of them all. That is the “justification” Paul speaks of when he says Christ “was raised again for our justification”, and it is why Romans 5 opens, “Therefore being justified by faith”. Who, according to the Old Testament, would be justified? Israel.

So when you read justification all throughout Paul’s letters, there should be no confusion about what he is talking about or who he is talking about. Abraham’s faith was imputed to him for righteousness, and “it was not written for his sake alone”, but for his seed who believe on him that raised up Jesus from the dead.

thread.label: Romans 5:1-11
thread.text: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:

classes.title: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.label: Ephesians 2:13-16
precepts.why:
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Christ came and died for his people; he was cut off for his people. Romans 5:9 says we are “justified by his blood”, and Ephesians says it is that same blood that brings near those who were far off.

“For he is our peace, who hath made both one”. That is the peace of Romans 5:1, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ”. And it shows who is being spoken of. Who is the both? The two nations. When you read the history in the book of Kings, Israel and Judah split apart into two kingdoms, and Ezekiel prophesied that our king would come and die for the nation of Israel and the nation of Judah, so that they would no longer be two nations but one nation under Christ.

He “hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”. What was two is now one new man, with no more division.

“And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross”. That is the same word as Romans 5:10, “we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son”. Reconcile means to bring together again, and the both being reconciled are the southern and northern kingdoms. So the audience in Romans is the same people God spoke to in the old covenant: the Jews in the church at Rome, and with them the Gentiles, who are the northern kingdom. Christ, by his death, brought both houses back to the Father as one.

precepts.label: 1 Chronicles 6:49
precepts.why:
Romans 5:11 says “by whom we have now received the atonement”, and the margin gives the word reconciliation. Atonement is Christ’s death, which brings us back to the Father. Reconcile in verse 10 and atonement in verse 11 are the same word; that is also called adoption. Atonement is reparation for a wrong or injury: when Christ died on the cross he died for our wrongs. Break the word down in English and it is at-onement: bringing back together again as one. Who did God come to bring together as one? Israel, the two sticks joined together, both kingdoms.

So who was the atonement ever made for? “But Aaron and his sons offered upon the altar of the burnt offering, and on the altar of incense, and were appointed for all the work of the place most holy, and to make an atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.” For Israel. Not for everybody.

The theology of the world says atonement is the reconciliation of God and all humankind. But God was never one with all humankind. All nations were never one with Israel, ever. The priesthood of Aaron made atonement for one people, and when Christ made the atonement with his own body, he made it for that same people.

precepts.label: 2 Chronicles 29:23-24
precepts.why:
In the days of Hezekiah, “they brought forth the he goats for the sin offering before the king and the congregation; and they laid their hands upon them: And the priests killed them, and they made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel: for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.”

All means all twelve, because Hezekiah was trying to bring them back together: all twelve tribes, and the strangers that showed up for the Passover.

Here reconciliation and atonement stand side by side, and they were made through the blood of animals. When Christ died, his body replaced them. That is why Romans 5:9 says “being now justified by his blood”: his blood replaces the animals, the works we no longer receive justification from. And the time came, as Daniel 9 foretold, when the temple was destroyed, the priests scattered abroad and not one stone left standing. With no way left to atone with animals, we had to have faith in Christ; otherwise you condemn yourself, indebted to a law you can no longer keep.

So atonement, reconciliation and justification are three words for the same thing, for the same people, with the same God. Reconciliation is the restoration of a friendly relationship, a reuniting; you cannot reunite with someone you were never joined to. Israel was with God before, rebelled until “he was turned to be their enemy”, and through the death of his Son was brought back again. That is Romans 5:10: “when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son”.

thread.label: Romans 5:8-11
thread.text: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
